THOUGHT: This is a chronic (10‑year) facial eruption of well‑demarcated, orange‑pink, flat‑topped papules and plaques with fine scale confined to forehead, cheeks, jawline and neck. The biopsy shows hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis, mild irregular psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, follicular hyperkeratosis, superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and mounds of parakeratosis alternating with orthokeratosis; importantly there is no interface dermatitis. Negative ANA/lupus markers and negative patch testing make lupus and allergic contact dermatitis less likely. The histologic pattern (psoriasiform hyperplasia with parakeratotic mounds and follicular hyperkeratosis) and the clinical plaque morphology strongly favor psoriasis (including facial or sebopsoriatic distribution). The reported clinical response to ustekinumab (an IL‑12/23 inhibitor used for psoriasis) further supports psoriasis as the leading diagnosis. Lack of interface change argues against discoid lupus and lichen planus; absence of atypical epidermotropic lymphocytes or dense Pautrier‑type infiltrate makes early mycosis fungoides less likely but it can rarely mimic chronic facial dermatoses. Seborrheic dermatitis / sebopsoriasis is a close mimic and remains an important alternative. Rosacea (including granulomatous rosacea) is considered given the facial localization but the histology and scaling favor psoriasiform processes.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Plaque psoriasis with predominant facial/sebopsoriatic involvement (facial psoriasis)
2. Sebopsoriasis / seborrheic dermatitis–psoriasis overlap
3. Chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discoid lupus) — less likely given absent interface change and negative serology
4. Early mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma) — can mimic chronic facial plaques but histology inconsistent
5. Rosacea (papulopustular/granulomatous subtype)
